These recommendations are subject to the local patterns of drug resistance WHO2 also recommends that for the small number of trav- ellers who would be unable to obtain prompt medical at- tention when malaria is suspected (within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms), it may be necessary to provide for a course of self-treatment (standby treatment). Clear in- structions must be given and persons taking standby med- ication must seek medical advice as soon as possible and resume any prophylaxis on completing the course. The ba- sis upon which the choice of prophylaxis is made (as de- tailed above) in turn broadly determines the appropriate choice of standby treatment. Thus one of the following treatment regimens can be used: • artemether-lumefantrine • atovaquone-proguanil • quinine plus doxycycline or clindamycin In each instance, prophylaxis should be resumed 1 week after the first standby treatment dose, except for meflo- quine prophylaxis which should be resumed at least 12 hours after the last treatment dose of quinine. In the USA, recommendations for prophylaxis are provid- ed by the CDC.15 For chloroquine-sensitive malaria, chlo- roquine alone is advised; hydroxychloroquine is suggested as an alternative. Travellers unable to take either of these 2 options should take atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone), doxycycline, or mefloquine. For all areas with chloro- quine-resistant malaria, 3 alternatives are available, meflo- quine, doxycycline, or atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone). Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) is recommended for emergency standby treatment. The use of primaquine is also advocated during the last 2 weeks of prophylaxis to prevent relapses due to P. vivax or P. ovale in persons re- turning from prolonged exposure in areas where relapsing malaria is endemic. UK experts16 have also published guidelines for the proph- ylaxis of malaria. In areas where P. falciparum is sensitive to chloroquine, travellers can either take chloroquine or proguanil for prophylaxis.
